name: Sustainable Business Fundamentals
description: A synthetic demo course about practical sustainability decisions in business.

topics.title: Systems thinking
topics.summary: Systems thinking looks beyond isolated events and studies how actors, resources, incentives, and feedback loops influence one another over time.
topics.worked_example: A company replaces plastic packaging with heavier glass. Packaging waste falls, but transport emissions rise. A systems view evaluates both effects before declaring the change an improvement.
topics.common_mistake: Optimizing one visible metric while ignoring effects elsewhere in the system.
topics.coach_question: What could happen outside the boundary of the metric you are optimizing?

topics.title: Stakeholder value
topics.summary: Stakeholder analysis identifies who affects or is affected by a decision, what each group values, and where interests align or conflict.
topics.worked_example: A supplier-code policy can reduce operational risk for a company while increasing compliance costs for small suppliers. The decision should account for both impact and influence.
topics.common_mistake: Treating every stakeholder as equally influential or assuming that influence and impact are the same.
topics.coach_question: Who carries the cost, who receives the benefit, and who can change the decision?

topics.title: Circular economy
topics.summary: A circular model aims to keep products and materials useful for longer through durability, repair, reuse, remanufacturing, and recycling.
topics.worked_example: A furniture company leases office chairs, repairs returned units, and reuses components. Revenue becomes service-based while material demand per customer falls.
topics.common_mistake: Equating circularity only with recycling at the end of a product's life.
topics.coach_question: How could the product retain value before recycling becomes necessary?

topics.title: Carbon accounting basics
topics.summary: Carbon accounting groups emissions into direct operations, purchased energy, and value-chain emissions so an organization can locate its largest sources and choose relevant actions.
topics.worked_example: Fuel burned in company vehicles is direct. Purchased electricity is energy-related. Emissions from suppliers and customer use sit in the wider value chain.
topics.common_mistake: Assuming the emissions a company controls directly are always its largest source.
topics.coach_question: Which emissions would disappear if the company stopped operating tomorrow, and which belong to its wider value chain?

questions.prompt: Which question best reflects systems thinking?
options: How might this change create effects elsewhere over time?
Which metric is easiest to improve this quarter?
How can the decision be implemented fastest?
questions.correct_answer: How might this change create effects elsewhere over time?
questions.explanation: Systems thinking examines relationships, delayed effects, and consequences beyond the immediately visible problem.

options: an output of a system later influences that same system
two departments use the same dashboard
a decision has a single measurable outcome
a manager asks employees for comments
questions.correct_answer: an output of a system later influences that same system
questions.explanation: A feedback loop occurs when a system's output returns as an input and changes future behavior.

questions.prompt: Why can improving one sustainability metric make the overall system worse?
questions.model_answer: The metric may use a narrow system boundary and ignore trade-offs or unintended consequences elsewhere.
questions.explanation: A local improvement is not necessarily a system improvement. Check boundaries, trade-offs, and delayed effects.

questions.prompt: Which pair is most useful when prioritizing stakeholders?
questions.explanation: Impact shows how strongly a group is affected; influence shows how strongly it can affect the decision.

questions.prompt: A material stakeholder interest is one that...
options: can meaningfully affect or be affected by the decision
questions.correct_answer: can meaningfully affect or be affected by the decision
questions.explanation: Materiality is about decision relevance and significant effects, not convenience or group size alone.

questions.prompt: What two questions help distinguish stakeholder impact from stakeholder influence?
questions.model_answer: Ask how strongly the stakeholder is affected and how strongly the stakeholder can change the decision.

rubric_points.label: Asks how strongly the stakeholder is affected
Asks how strongly the stakeholder can affect the decision

questions.explanation: Impact runs from the decision to the stakeholder; influence runs from the stakeholder to the decision.

questions.prompt: Which action usually preserves the most product value?
questions.explanation: Repair and reuse preserve the product, its components, and the energy already invested in manufacturing.

questions.prompt: Which business model most directly supports product return and refurbishment?
questions.explanation: When the provider retains ownership, it has a direct incentive to recover, maintain, and refurbish products.

questions.prompt: Name two design choices that can keep a product useful for longer.
questions.model_answer: Examples include durable components and a modular design that makes repair or replacement easier.
questions.explanation: Circular design delays disposal by preserving product and component value before recycling is needed.

questions.prompt: Fuel burned in company-owned delivery vans is usually classified as...
questions.explanation: Scope 1 covers direct emissions from sources the organization owns or controls.

questions.prompt: Emissions associated with purchased electricity are usually...
questions.explanation: Scope 2 covers indirect emissions from purchased electricity, steam, heating, or cooling.

questions.prompt: Briefly distinguish Scope 1, Scope 2, and Scope 3 emissions.
questions.model_answer: Scope 1 is direct operational emissions, Scope 2 is purchased energy, and Scope 3 covers other value-chain emissions.
questions.explanation: The three scopes distinguish direct operations, purchased energy, and the wider value chain.
